GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrexia of U:
Fever is a measured pyrexia; the task is to separate the septic patient needing immediate treatment from an undifferentiated or prolonged fever needing a staged search.
  • First exclude the emergencies: sepsis (fever with organ dysfunction → the Sepsis 6) (see sepsis), meningococcal disease (fever + a non-blanching rash) (see meningococcal disease) and neutropenic sepsis in the recently chemotherapy-treated patient (see neutropenic sepsis).
  • When a fever >38.3°C persists for >3 weeks and is undiagnosed after initial workup, it is a pyrexia of unknown origin (see pyrexia of unknown origin), whose causes are infection, malignancy, connective-tissue disease and miscellaneous.
  • Foreground lymphoma / leukaemia (see lymphoma), TB (see tuberculosis), infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis) and the returning traveller (see fever in the returning traveller, returning traveller). The rule: treat sepsis now, then investigate systematically.
🚨Treat sepsis before you chase the source. Fever with any organ dysfunction, hypotension or a raised lactate is sepsis — take blood cultures and lactate, give oxygen, IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics (the Sepsis 6) within the hour (see sepsis). A non-blanching purpuric rash with fever is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise — give antibiotics immediately (see meningococcal disease). A fever in a patient within weeks of chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis — a medical emergency treated within one hour (see neutropenic sepsis). Beware the frail elderly, who may be septic without a fever.

🟠Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO)
  • Fever >38.3°C for >3 weeks, undiagnosed after initial inpatient / outpatient workup
  • Causes: infection, malignancy, connective-tissue disease, miscellaneous (see PUO)
  • Needs a structured, staged search — not blind antibiotics
🟠Malignancy (lymphoma / leukaemia)
  • Fever + night sweats + weight loss + lymphadenopathy → lymphoma (see lymphoma)
  • Fever + fatigue + bruising + cytopenias → leukaemia (see leukaemia)
  • B symptoms are a red-flag cluster demanding imaging + biopsy
🩹Chronic infection (TB / endocarditis)
  • Fever + chronic cough + weight loss → TB (see tuberculosis)
  • Fever + a new murmur + emboli → infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis)
  • Deep abscess, osteomyelitis and biliary sepsis also smoulder
🩹The returning traveller
  • Fever after tropical travel is malaria until excluded (see fever in the returning traveller)
  • Take a full travel, exposure and prophylaxis history (see returning traveller)
  • Also enteric fever, dengue, viral haemorrhagic fevers, hepatitis
Sepsis first, then a staged search. Resuscitate and treat sepsis, meningococcal disease and neutropenic sepsis immediately. Only once the emergencies are excluded and the fever persists undiagnosed do you work it up as a PUO — infection, malignancy or connective-tissue disease.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss:
Unintentional weight loss — clinically significant at >5% of body weight over 6–12 months — demands a cause be found before it is blamed on age or mood. The red-flag cluster is weight loss with anorexia, night sweats or a mass, which points to malignancy (GI — colorectal, gastric, pancreatic; lung; haematological) (see colorectal cancer, lymphoma) and to chronic infection such as TB or HIV (see tuberculosis, HIV). Metabolic causes are common: hyperthyroidism (weight loss despite a good appetite) (see hyperthyroidism), new diabetes (polyuria + polydipsia) (see type 1 diabetes) and malabsorption (coeliac, pancreatic insufficiency) (see coeliac disease). Do not forget the psychosocial — depression, eating disorders and poverty (see depressive disorders, eating disorders). Quantify the loss, screen broadly and investigate the red flags urgently, and beware cachexia (see cachexia).
🚨Unexplained weight loss is a cancer red flag. Weight loss with anorexia, night sweats, a mass or lymphadenopathy mandates urgent investigation for malignancy (see colorectal cancer, lymphoma). Weight loss with fever and night sweats raises TB and HIV (see tuberculosis, HIV). Rapid weight loss with polyuria, polydipsia and ketosis is new type 1 diabetes that can progress to DKA (see type 1 diabetes). Never attribute weight loss to depression or age until organic disease is excluded — the mistake costs late diagnoses.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tiredness:
Fatigue is one of the commonest presentations; most is benign, but a minority hides serious organic disease.
  • Screen first for the red-flag cluster — fatigue with weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy or bleeding points to malignancy / haematological disease (see lymphoma, leukaemia).
  • The common treatable organic causes are anaemia (see anaemia), hypothyroidism (see hypothyroidism), diabetes (see type 2 diabetes), chronic kidney / liver / heart disease, coeliac disease and sleep apnoea (see snoring & apnoeas). The commonest single cause is psychological — depression and anxiety (see depressive disorders).
  • Consider Addison’s in fatigue with postural dizziness and pigmentation (see Addison’s disease), and medications. Chronic fatigue syndrome is a positive diagnosis made only after exclusion (see chronic fatigue syndrome).
🚨Do not miss the sinister cause of fatigue. Fatigue with weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, bone pain or easy bruising / bleeding points to lymphoma, leukaemia or myeloma and needs urgent bloods and a film (see leukaemia, myeloma). Fatigue with breathlessness and pallor may be severe anaemia (see anaemia). Fatigue with postural collapse, pigmentation, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia may be an Addisonian crisis (see Addison’s disease). Never diagnose chronic fatigue syndrome without first excluding organic disease.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Malaise:
Lethargy and malaise are a vague sense of being unwell or run down — often the earliest, non-specific herald of significant illness, especially in the elderly.
  • In the frail, older or immunosuppressed patient, malaise may be the only sign of sepsis or a metabolic emergency — check observations, glucose, U&E and calcium early (see sepsis).
  • Organic causes overlap with fatigue: anaemia (see anaemia), thyroid disease (see hypothyroidism), diabetes, renal / hepatic failure (see chronic kidney disease), occult infection — EBV, HIV, hepatitis (see viral infections, HIV) — malignancy and adrenal insufficiency (see Addison’s disease).
  • Psychological and iatrogenic causes — depression and medications — are common (see depressive disorders, polypharmacy). Never dismiss malaise in the vulnerable.
🚨Malaise in the vulnerable is an emergency until proven otherwise. In the frail, older or immunosuppressed, malaise with a fever, tachycardia or new confusion may be the only sign of sepsis — septic-screen with a low threshold (see sepsis). Malaise can be the face of a metabolic emergency — DKA, hypercalcaemia, hyponatraemia, an Addisonian crisis or uraemia — so check glucose, U&E and calcium early (see Addison’s disease, hypercalcaemia). Do not label a run-down elderly patient as “just tired” without observations and basic bloods.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised Lymphade:
Generalised lymphadenopathy is enlarged nodes in two or more non-contiguous regions — distinct from a single or regional node (see localised lymphadenopathy).
  • The must-not-miss is haematological malignancy — lymphoma (painless rubbery nodes + B symptoms) (see lymphoma) and leukaemia (nodes + cytopenias / bruising) (see leukaemia) — both needing a tissue diagnosis.
  • The commonest cause is infective: EBV / CMV (young, sore throat, splenomegaly), HIV seroconversion, TB and toxoplasmosis (see viral infections, HIV, tuberculosis).
  • Immunological causes include SLE / connective-tissue disease and sarcoidosis (see connective-tissue disease, sarcoidosis); also consider drug reactions and metastatic malignancy. Assess associated splenomegaly (see splenomegaly). A persistent, hard, fixed or B-symptom node needs urgent biopsy.

Painless, rubbery, generalised nodes with night sweats, weight loss or fever (B symptoms) point to lymphoma and demand an excision node biopsy, not a fine-needle aspirate (see lymphoma). Nodes with bruising, pallor and abnormal counts suggest leukaemia (see leukaemia). Red-flag features — >2 cm, hard, fixed, supraclavicular, or persisting beyond 4–6 weeks — warrant urgent referral. Do not wait out a suspicious node on repeated courses of antibiotics.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats:
True night sweats are drenching sweats that soak nightclothes and bedding — a classic B symptom that must be taken seriously when persistent. The must-not-miss cluster is night sweats with weight loss and fever, pointing to lymphoma / leukaemia (see lymphoma, leukaemia), TB (see tuberculosis) and infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis). Consider HIV and deep infection (see HIV), and endocrine causes such as hyperthyroidism and phaeochromocytoma (see hyperthyroidism). The commonest benign causes are menopause (vasomotor flushes) (see menopausal symptoms), nocturnal hypoglycaemia in treated diabetes (see type 1 diabetes), medications (SSRIs, opioids) (see polypharmacy), GORD and anxiety. Distinguish these from the drenching, B-symptom pattern that demands a search for malignancy and infection.
🚨Drenching night sweats with weight loss are a red flag. Persistent night sweats soaking the bedding, with weight loss and fever, point to lymphoma or leukaemia and mandate a FBC, film, LDH and imaging (see lymphoma). Night sweats with a chronic cough and haemoptysis suggest TB (see tuberculosis); with a new murmur and fever, infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis). Do not reassure a patient with true drenching sweats and systemic symptoms as “menopause” or “stress” before excluding malignancy and infection.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appetite:
Loss of appetite (anorexia) is a reduced desire to eat — important as an early, non-specific marker of serious organic disease, and distinct from anorexia nervosa.
  • The must-not-miss causes are malignancy (the anorexia–cachexia syndrome) (see colorectal cancer, lymphoma, cachexia) and occult sepsis in the frail elderly (see sepsis).
  • GI and metabolic causes are common: peptic / gastric disease and dysphagia (see dyspepsia), hepatic / renal failure (see chronic kidney disease), hypercalcaemia (see hypercalcaemia), hyponatraemia, Addison’s and hypothyroidism.
  • Do not forget the psychiatric and iatrogenic — depression, a leading cause (see depressive disorders), eating disorders in the young (see eating disorders), dementia / frailty, and appetite-suppressing drugs (see polypharmacy). Quantify intake and weight, and support nutrition (see malnutrition).
🚨New anorexia can be the first sign of cancer or sepsis. Loss of appetite with weight loss and cachexia warrants a search for malignancy (see colorectal cancer). In a frail elderly patient, anorexia may be the only new symptom of occult sepsis or a metabolic derangement — check observations, glucose, U&E and calcium (see sepsis, hypercalcaemia). In the young, a fear of weight gain and distorted body image points to an eating disorder needing specialist assessment and monitoring for refeeding risk (see eating disorders). Weigh the patient and quantify intake — do not accept “poor appetite” without a cause.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls:
Falls in older adults are usually multifactorial; the job is to separate a mechanical trip from a fall that signals cardiac, neurological or acute medical disease.
  • For the broader geriatric approach, see falls in the elderly. A fall with true loss of consciousness suggests cardiac syncope — arrhythmia, aortic stenosis or PE (see syncope, valvular heart disease).
  • Always look hard for injury (head injury on anticoagulants, a neck-of-femur fracture) (see NOF fracture) and for a fall as the presentation of sepsis, MI or stroke (see sepsis).
  • The common contributors are postural hypotension and culprit medications (see polypharmacy), gait / balance and neurological disorders, visual impairment, arthritis, deconditioning and environmental hazards. Assess every domain and treat reversible factors (see falls assessment, frailty).
🚨A fall can be syncope, injury or acute illness in disguise. A fall with loss of consciousness, no warning or on exertion may be cardiac syncope — arrhythmia or aortic stenosis — and needs a 12-lead ECG (see syncope, valvular heart disease). A head strike on anticoagulants risks intracranial haemorrhage (see reduced consciousness); a painful, shortened and externally rotated leg is a neck-of-femur fracture (see NOF fracture). A fall with new confusion and fever may be the presentation of sepsis (see sepsis). Examine for injury and screen for an acute medical cause in every faller.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Frailty & Functional:
Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve; the key rule is that “acopia” is never a diagnosis — always find the cause of decline.
  • An acute or subacute decline (“off legs”) is acute illness until proven otherwise — sepsis, MI, stroke, AKI, delirium and medication toxicity all present this way (see off legs, sepsis, delirium).
  • Grade frailty with the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale (see frailty) and recognise the frailty syndromes — falls, immobility, incontinence and delirium.
  • Address the contributors: polypharmacy (see polypharmacy), malnutrition / sarcopenia (see malnutrition), cognitive impairment (see dementia), depression (see depressive disorders) and social factors. The framework is the Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (see comprehensive geriatric assessment) — multidisciplinary, aiming to restore function.
🚨“Off legs” is acute illness until proven otherwise. A sudden or subacute functional decline in an older person is a presentation of sepsis, MI, stroke, AKI, delirium or drug toxicity — not simply “social” (see off legs, sepsis). Delirium — acute, fluctuating inattention — is common, dangerous and reversible; screen with the 4AT and find the cause (see delirium). GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained Collapse:
An unexplained collapse is a transient loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery; the first task is to separate cardiac syncope from neurological and reflex causes (see transient loss of consciousness, syncope). Cardiac syncope kills — arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, HOCM and PE cause sudden, exertional or unheralded collapse, and a 12-lead ECG is mandatory in every patient (see valvular heart disease, pulmonary embolism). The commonest causes are reflex (vasovagal) and orthostatic hypotension (see syncope). Distinguish a seizure (tongue-biting, post-ictal confusion) (see seizures) and hypoglycaemia (see type 1 diabetes) from true syncope. Take an eyewitness history, do an ECG and a lying / standing BP, and refer red-flag features urgently.
🚨A 12-lead ECG is mandatory in every collapse. Red-flag features — collapse on exertion, without warning, causing injury, or with a family history of sudden cardiac death or an abnormal ECG — point to cardiac syncope (arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, HOCM) and need urgent cardiology (see syncope, valvular heart disease). Collapse with breathlessness, hypoxia or pleuritic pain may be PE (see pulmonary embolism). Do not attribute a collapse to a “simple faint” without an eyewitness account, an ECG and a lying / standing blood pressure.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised / System:
Generalised oedema is bilateral, dependent, pitting fluid overload; the first split is systemic (bilateral) versus localised (unilateral — DVT, cellulitis, lymphoedema) (see swollen leg).
  • The three great causes are cardiac (heart failure) (see chronic heart failure), renal (nephrotic syndrome, CKD) (see glomerulonephritis) and hepatic (cirrhosis) (see liver cirrhosis) — plus hypoalbuminaemia from malnutrition or protein loss (see malnutrition).
  • Read the pattern: nephrotic oedema is periorbital with frothy urine (see proteinuria, periorbital oedema); hepatic oedema comes with ascites and chronic-liver stigmata (see ascites).
  • Also consider drugs (calcium-channel blockers, NSAIDs, steroids) and venous disease (see polypharmacy). Urgently treat pulmonary oedema, and never mistake a unilateral hot leg for systemic overload.
🚨Two traps in generalised oedema. First, cardiac failure with pulmonary oedema — bilateral pitting oedema with orthopnoea, a raised JVP and lung crepitations — needs urgent treatment (see acute heart failure). Second, never mistake a unilateral hot, swollen, tender leg (a DVT) for systemic oedema — it needs a Doppler and anticoagulation, not diuretics (see swollen leg, DVT / PE). And sudden facial and tongue swelling is angioedema / anaphylaxis, not dependent oedema, and can obstruct the airway (see anaphylaxis). Bilateral, dependent and pitting is systemic; unilateral or acute facial is not.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration & Fluid:
Dehydration and fluid depletion are a deficit of body water ± sodium; assess severity and find the cause.
  • Grade the deficit clinically — observations, mucous membranes, capillary refill, skin turgor, urine output and urea. The emergency is hypovolaemic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, a raised lactate) needing immediate fluid resuscitation (see shock, shock assessment).
  • Behind severe depletion, think DKA / HHS (see type 1 diabetes), a GI catastrophe and sepsis (see sepsis).
  • The causes are losses — GI (vomiting, diarrhoea, high-output stoma) (see diarrhoea), renal (diuretics, osmotic diuresis, diabetes insipidus, Addison’s) (see diabetes insipidus, Addison’s disease) and skin — and reduced intake / redistribution (frail elderly, third-spacing in pancreatitis) (see frailty, acute pancreatitis). Resuscitate, then replace the deficit and ongoing losses (see acute kidney injury).
🚨Hypovolaemic shock needs immediate fluid resuscitation. Tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria and a raised lactate signal shock — give a fluid challenge and reassess, and identify the source of loss (see shock). Behind severe depletion, think DKA / HHS (thirst, ketones, high glucose) (see type 1 diabetes), a GI catastrophe (bleeding, obstruction) and sepsis with distributive loss (see sepsis). In the frail elderly, dehydration presents as confusion, a raised urea and pre-renal AKI (see acute kidney injury). Match the fluid to the deficit and the electrolytes — do not under-resuscitate a shocked patient.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia:
Cachexia is a complex metabolic wasting syndrome — loss of skeletal muscle (with or without fat) driven by inflammatory cytokines — that is NOT fully reversed by feeding, and it is always a marker of serious underlying disease.
  • Distinguish it from simple weight loss or starvation, which responds to nutrition (see weight loss, malnutrition).
  • The dominant fear is occult malignancy — lung, GI and pancreatic cancer (see lung cancer, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer) — and chronic infection such as TB or HIV (see tuberculosis, HIV).
  • Advanced organ failure produces its own cachexia: cardiac (see chronic heart failure), respiratory (see COPD) and renal (see chronic kidney disease), each a poor-prognosis marker. In the elderly it overlaps with frailty and sarcopenia (see frailty). Quantify the loss, screen broadly, and hunt the underlying cause.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised Itch:
Generalised itch (pruritus) splits by one question: is there a primary rash?
  • Itch with a rash is usually dermatological — eczema, psoriasis, urticaria, scabies (see eczema, psoriasis, scabies, pruritus).
  • Itch without a rash (only excoriations) mandates a hunt for systemic disease. The sinister causes are malignancy — lymphoma (itch, sometimes after alcohol) and polycythaemia (aquagenic itch after a warm bath) (see lymphoma, polycythaemia) — and cholestasis (see primary biliary cholangitis, jaundice).
  • The other systemic causes are CKD / uraemia (see chronic kidney disease), iron deficiency (see anaemia), thyroid disease (see hyperthyroidism) and drugs (see drug reactions). Examine the skin, screen the bloods, and treat the cause.
🚨Itch without a rash can be the first sign of cancer. Persistent generalised itch with no primary skin lesion, especially with weight loss, night sweats or lymphadenopathy, may herald lymphoma (see lymphoma); itch after a warm bath with a ruddy complexion suggests polycythaemia (see polycythaemia). Itch with jaundice, pale stools and dark urine is cholestasis / biliary obstruction and can signal pancreatic cancer (see jaundice). Do not treat chronic itch symptomatically without excluding these systemic causes.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessness:
Breathlessness (dyspnoea) is triaged first by tempo — acute (minutes to hours) versus chronic (weeks to months) — and acute breathlessness with hypoxia is an emergency.
  • The immediately life-threatening acute causes are PE (see pulmonary embolism), tension pneumothorax (see pneumothorax), acute pulmonary oedema from heart failure (see acute heart failure), acute severe asthma (see asthma), anaphylaxis (see anaphylaxis), ACS (see acute coronary syndrome) and DKA (Kussmaul breathing) (see type 1 diabetes).
  • Common causes are pneumonia (see pneumonia) and COPD (see COPD); do not forget severe anaemia (see anaemia). Chronic breathlessness spans COPD, heart failure, ILD (see interstitial lung disease) and lung cancer (see lung cancer).
  • Check SpO2, give oxygen, and treat the specific cause (see increased work of breathing).
🚨Hypoxia kills — treat before you finish diagnosing. Give oxygen, assess ABCDE and get an ABG. A sudden unilateral silent chest with tracheal deviation and shock is a tension pneumothorax — needle decompress immediately (see pneumothorax). Wheeze, urticaria and angioedema after a trigger is anaphylaxis — give IM adrenaline (see anaphylaxis). A silent chest in asthma is peri-arrest (see asthma). In COPD, target SpO2 88–92% and beware CO2 retention (see CO₂ retention signs).

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / Light-he:
“Dizziness” must first be parsed: this topic is the PRESYNCOPAL, systemic lens — a feeling of faintness or light-headedness — as distinct from vertigo, the illusion of movement.
  • The dangerous presyncopal cause is cardiac — arrhythmia (tachy- or bradyarrhythmia / heart block) and structural disease (aortic stenosis) (see tachycardia, bradycardia / heart block, syncope & pre-syncope).
  • Systemic causes are common: postural (orthostatic) hypotension (drugs, dehydration, autonomic), anaemia (see anaemia), an occult GI bleed (see GI bleed) and hypoglycaemia in the treated diabetic (see diabetes treatments).
  • If the complaint is truly the room spinning, follow the vertigo / neurological workup instead (see dizziness & vertigo). Check lying/standing BP, an ECG, glucose and FBC.
🚨Cardiac presyncope can precede sudden death. Light-headedness on exertion, with palpitations or chest pain, or leading to collapse, points to an arrhythmia, heart block or aortic stenosis — get an ECG and consider ambulatory monitoring and an echo (see tachycardia, bradycardia / heart block). Light-headedness with pallor or melaena may be an occult GI bleed / severe anaemia (see GI bleed). In a diabetic on insulin or a sulfonylurea, always check a capillary glucose (see diabetes treatments).

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis:
Cyanosis is a bluish discolouration appearing when there is >50 g/L of deoxygenated haemoglobin; the first split is CENTRAL versus PERIPHERAL.
  • Central cyanosis (blue tongue and lips) reflects systemic hypoxaemia or abnormal haemoglobin — from respiratory failure (see respiratory failure), a right-to-left cardiac shunt (cyanotic congenital heart disease) (see congenital heart disease), or methaemoglobinaemia (cyanosis that does not correct with oxygen) (see toxicology).
  • Peripheral cyanosis (blue fingers / toes, normal tongue) reflects poor local perfusion — cold, low cardiac output, shock, peripheral vascular disease or Raynaud’s (see Raynaud’s phenomenon).
  • Polycythaemia deepens the colour and anaemia masks it (see polycythaemia). Check SpO2 and an ABG, give oxygen, and treat the cause (see cyanosis).
🚨Central cyanosis means dangerous hypoxaemia until proven otherwise. A blue tongue and lips with a low SpO2 is systemic hypoxaemia — give oxygen, get an ABG and escalate (see respiratory failure). A cyanosed neonate / infant, especially on crying, is cyanotic congenital heart disease until excluded (see congenital heart disease). If the patient is cyanosed with a low SpO2 but a normal PaO2 and does not pink up on oxygen, suspect methaemoglobinaemia (culprit drugs such as dapsone / nitrites) — it needs methylene blue (see toxicology).

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing:
Finger clubbing is loss of the normal nail-fold angle with a boggy, fluctuant nail bed and increased nail curvature — a physical sign that flags serious cardiorespiratory, GI or hepatic disease.
  • The cardiorespiratory causes dominate: lung cancer and suppurative lung disease (see lung cancer), bronchiectasis (see bronchiectasis), ILD / pulmonary fibrosis (see interstitial lung disease), cystic fibrosis, cyanotic congenital heart disease (see congenital heart disease) and infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis).
  • The GI / hepatic causes are IBD (see inflammatory bowel disease), coeliac disease (see coeliac disease) and cirrhosis (see liver cirrhosis).
  • Also consider thyroid acropachy (Graves) (see hyperthyroidism) and familial or unilateral (vascular) clubbing. Clubbing is a clue — find the disease behind it.
🚨New clubbing is a red flag for lung cancer and other serious disease. Clubbing in a smoker with weight loss, haemoptysis or a cough mandates a CXR and a low threshold for CT — lung cancer until excluded (see lung cancer). Clubbing with fever, a new murmur and emboli (splinter haemorrhages, Osler’s nodes) is infective endocarditis — take blood cultures and echo (see infective endocarditis). Clubbing plus painful wrists / ankles (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy) strengthens the case for an underlying lung malignancy.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor:
Pallor is pale skin and mucous membranes — best judged at the conjunctivae, palmar creases and tongue — and the key question is whether it reflects anaemia, acute blood loss, or simple vasoconstriction. The emergency is acute haemorrhage / shock: pallor with tachycardia and hypotension means bleeding until proven otherwise (GI bleed, trauma, ruptured AAA, ruptured ectopic) (see GI bleed, shock). Otherwise think anaemia and its cause — iron deficiency (find the bleeding source, including GI malignancy and menorrhagia) (see anaemia, colorectal cancer, koilonychia), B12 / folate, chronic disease, haemolysis, and marrow failure / leukaemia (see leukaemia). Non-anaemic pallor comes from vasoconstriction and hypothyroidism (see hypothyroidism). Confirm anaemia with an FBC before you reassure.
🚨Sudden pallor with shock is haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Pallor + tachycardia + hypotension → resuscitate and find the bleeding — GI haemorrhage (melaena, haematemesis), trauma, a ruptured AAA or a ruptured ectopic (see GI bleed). In the stable patient, iron-deficiency anaemia must have its source found — never blame diet without excluding GI malignancy (see colorectal cancer). Pallor with bruising and recurrent infection suggests marrow failure / leukaemia and needs an urgent film (see leukaemia).

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classificatio:
Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery; the task is to resuscitate with an ABCDE approach while classifying it into the four types. Distributive shock — septic (see sepsis), anaphylactic (see anaphylaxis) and neurogenic — is warm with vasodilatation. Obstructive shock — massive PE (see pulmonary embolism), cardiac tamponade (see pericarditis) and tension pneumothorax (see pneumothorax) — blocks the circulation mechanically. Hypovolaemic shock is haemorrhagic (trauma, GI bleed, ruptured AAA / ectopic) or fluid loss (see GI bleed, fluid therapy), and cardiogenic shock is pump failure (large MI, arrhythmia, acute valve lesion) (see acute coronary syndrome, acute heart failure). A raised lactate marks hypoperfusion — recognise shock early (see shock (types)).
🚨Distributive and obstructive shock kill fast and need cause-specific treatment now. Septic shock → the Sepsis 6 within the hour (see sepsis); anaphylactic shock → IM adrenaline immediately (see anaphylaxis). Tension pneumothorax → needle / finger decompression (see pneumothorax); tamponade → pericardiocentesis (see pericarditis); massive PE → consider thrombolysis (see pulmonary embolism). Fluids help hypovolaemic and (initially) distributive shock but can worsen cardiogenic and obstructive shock — classify while you resuscitate. A raised lactate is your early warning.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Acute Fun:
“Off legs” — a sudden loss of mobility or independence in an older person — is ACUTE ILLNESS until proven otherwise, and must never be dismissed as “acopia”. The commonest hidden cause is sepsis, often from a UTI or pneumonia (see sepsis, urinary tract infection, pneumonia). Other emergencies present silently: MI (see acute coronary syndrome), stroke (see stroke / TIA) and cord compression (see spinal cord disorders). Reversible drivers include electrolyte disturbance and AKI (see electrolyte disturbances, acute kidney injury), medications / polypharmacy (see polypharmacy), and occult injury such as a fractured hip (see neck of femur fracture). Set it against frailty and delirium (see frailty, delirium), and assess with a CGA (see comprehensive geriatric assessment).
🚨“Off legs” is a presentation, not a diagnosis — and “acopia” / “social admission” are dangerous labels. An older person going off their legs may be septic (UTI, pneumonia) with few localising signs (see sepsis), or have a silent MI, a stroke or cord compression (see stroke / TIA, spinal cord disorders). Always check observations, glucose, U&E, calcium and an ECG, examine for a fractured hip (see neck of femur fracture) and review the drug chart before attributing decline to age or social factors.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sores:
Pressure sores (pressure ulcers / injuries) are localised skin and soft-tissue damage over a bony prominence caused by sustained pressure and shear; grade the depth and act hard on prevention. They are staged category 1–4 plus unstageable and deep-tissue injury (see pressure sores). The dangerous complication is infection — a colonised ulcer can progress to cellulitis, osteomyelitis and systemic sepsis (see sepsis, bone & joint infection). Prevention rests on risk assessment (Waterlow / Braden), repositioning, pressure-relieving surfaces, skin care, continence and nutrition (see malnutrition, frailty). Crucially, pressure damage can be a marker of neglect — consider safeguarding (see adult safeguarding). Distinguish true pressure ulcers from moisture lesions and leg ulcers (see leg ulcers & pressure injury).
🚨An infected pressure ulcer can become life-threatening sepsis — and pressure damage is a red flag for neglect. Spreading erythema, purulent discharge, fever or a rising NEWS around an ulcer means cellulitis or sepsis (see sepsis); a deep ulcer that probes to bone or fails to heal suggests osteomyelitis (see bone & joint infection). Severe or multiple avoidable pressure ulcers, especially with other signs of poor care, warrant a safeguarding referral (see adult safeguarding). Prevention is the priority — assess risk and act before the skin breaks.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia:
Hypothermia is a core temperature below 35°C, measured with a low-reading thermometer, and it is graded mild (32–35°C), moderate (28–32°C) and severe (<28°C).
  • Always seek a precipitant as well as treating the cold: sepsis can present with hypothermia rather than fever (see sepsis); check for hypoglycaemia (see type 1 diabetes), myxoedema coma (see hypothyroidism), an Addisonian crisis (see Addison’s disease) and drug / alcohol intoxication (see toxicology).
  • Environmental exposure and impaired thermoregulation dominate in the frail elderly at home and in immersion (see frailty, hyperthermia / hypothermia).
  • The ECG may show J (Osborn) waves and bradyarrhythmias, and the great danger is ventricular fibrillation triggered by rough handling — handle gently.
🚨Handle the severely hypothermic patient gently — and do not declare death until warm. Below about 30°C the myocardium is irritable and prone to ventricular fibrillation, which can be triggered by rough movement; monitor, avoid unnecessary jolts, and rewarm in a controlled way (see hyperthermia / hypothermia). Remember “not dead until warm and dead” — continue resuscitation while rewarming. Always exclude an underlying sepsis (see sepsis), hypoglycaemia, myxoedema or Addisonian cause, and beware afterdrop and arrhythmias during rewarming.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia / Heat:
Hyperthermia is a raised core temperature from failed thermoregulation — NOT a regulated fever — and the key split is heat exhaustion versus life-threatening heat stroke.
  • Heat stroke (core >40°C with CNS dysfunction: confusion, seizures, coma) causes multi-organ failure and needs immediate aggressive cooling (see hyperthermia / hypothermia). Heat exhaustion (core <40°C, sweating, intact cognition) is milder.
  • Crucially, several drug and endocrine emergencies also cause hyperthermia: neuroleptic malignant syndrome (see neuroleptic malignant syndrome), serotonin syndrome and malignant hyperthermia (see toxicology) and thyroid storm (see hyperthyroidism).
  • Always distinguish these from a regulated fever due to sepsis (see sepsis), whose mechanism and treatment differ. Watch for rhabdomyolysis, AKI and DIC.
🚨Heat stroke is a cooling emergency — and the hyperthermic toxidromes need their specific antidotes. Core >40°C with altered mental state → cool rapidly (evaporative / cold-water immersion) and support organs (see hyperthermia / hypothermia). Rigidity on an antipsychotic with a raised CK is NMS (see neuroleptic malignant syndrome); clonus and hyperreflexia on serotonergic drugs is serotonin syndrome; muscle rigidity during anaesthesia is malignant hyperthermia (dantrolene) (see toxicology); AF, tremor and agitation in Graves’ is thyroid storm (see hyperthyroidism). Do not mistake sepsis for heat illness — or vice versa.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse / Safegu:
A safeguarding concern arises when injury, neglect or a presentation pattern signals harm to an adult at risk — the clinician’s duty is to recognise it and act on the safeguarding pathway.
  • Abuse takes many forms: physical, neglect / acts of omission, self-neglect, financial or material, psychological / emotional, sexual, discriminatory, organisational, domestic abuse and modern slavery.
  • The alarms are an unexplained or patterned injury, a history that is inconsistent with the injury or changes between tellings, delayed presentation, and signs of neglect — pressure sores (see pressure sores, pressure sores), dehydration (see dehydration) and malnutrition. Watch for financial exploitation and a stressed or controlling carer.
  • Always assess mental capacity (Mental Capacity Act) and whether a person lacking capacity is being deprived of their liberty (see DoLS). Document meticulously and make a safeguarding referral to the local authority under the Care Act 2014 (see elder abuse / adult safeguarding).
🚨An unexplained injury or neglect in a vulnerable adult is a safeguarding emergency. Patterned bruising (grip or ligature marks), injuries of different ages, or an injury that does not fit the history must not be explained away — examine, document with body maps and photographs, and protect the patient (see elder abuse / adult safeguarding). Severe pressure sores, dehydration and malnutrition in a dependent person are life-threatening neglect (see pressure sores). Assess capacity and act in the person’s best interests. Safeguarding is everyone’s duty — never discharge an adult at risk without raising the concern.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The Septic:
Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection — the deteriorating patient must be recognised early and treated with the Sepsis 6 within one hour (see sepsis). Screen every unwell patient with NEWS2 and qSOFA (respiratory rate ≥22, systolic BP ≤100 mmHg, altered mentation); rising scores, hypotension or a raised lactate mark severity. Septic shock is vasopressor-requiring hypotension with a lactate >2 mmol/L despite fluid resuscitation. The Sepsis 6 is three in (oxygen, IV fluids, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics) and three out (blood cultures, lactate, urine-output monitoring). Always identify and control the source. Two forms are can’t-miss: neutropenic sepsis after chemotherapy (see neutropenic sepsis) and meningococcal sepsis with a non-blanching rash (see meningococcal disease). The frail elderly may be septic without a fever.
🚨Sepsis is a time-critical emergency — deliver the Sepsis 6 within one hour. Infection with hypotension, a raised lactate, new confusion, oliguria or an escalating NEWS2 is sepsis — do not delay antibiotics and fluids (see sepsis). Fever within weeks of chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis — give antibiotics within the hour, before the neutrophil count is back (see neutropenic sepsis). A non-blanching purpuric rash is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise (see meningococcal disease). Escalate the deteriorating patient to a senior and to critical care early, and watch for evolving shock and AKI (see shock, acute kidney injury).

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the Returni:
Fever after recent travel is malaria until excluded — the history of geography, incubation period and exposures directs the search.
  • See fever in the returning traveller for the full approach. Malaria (especially falciparum) can kill within days and needs thick and thin blood films, repeated up to three times if negative (see malaria).
  • Consider enteric fever (typhoid) from the Indian subcontinent (see enteric fever), dengue and other arboviruses, viral haemorrhagic fever — which demands isolation and notification — viral hepatitis (see viral hepatitis) and travellers’ diarrhoea (see diarrhoea).
  • Match the incubation period to the illness: short (<10 days) suggests dengue, arboviruses and early VHF; typhoid and malaria are intermediate; malaria and TB may present months later. Do not forget cosmopolitan causes and HIV seroconversion (see HIV), and always take a pre-travel prophylaxis and vaccination history (see travel medicine / malaria prophylaxis).
🚨Every fever after tropical travel is malaria until the films are negative. Falciparum malaria can progress to cerebral malaria, shock and death within days — send thick and thin films urgently and repeat them (see malaria). A fever with bleeding and travel to an endemic area within 21 days may be a viral haemorrhagic fever — isolate the patient, use strict infection control, and notify the authorities before extensive testing. A non-blanching rash is meningococcal disease (see meningococcal disease), and any traveller can still develop sepsis from a cosmopolitan source (see sepsis). Take a meticulous travel, exposure and prophylaxis history.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Infections:
Recurrent, severe, unusual or persistent infections raise the question of immunodeficiency — and the pattern of organism points to the defect (see immune system overview & immunodeficiency). Secondary immunodeficiency is far commoner: HIV (see HIV), hyposplenism (asplenia, sickle cell), neutropenia (chemotherapy, haematological disease) (see neutropenic sepsis), hypogammaglobulinaemia (myeloma, protein loss, drugs), diabetes, malnutrition and immunosuppressants. Primary immunodeficiency includes antibody defects (CVID, X-linked agammaglobulinaemia), combined T-cell defects (SCID), phagocyte defects (chronic granulomatous disease) and complement deficiency. The organism names the defect: encapsulated bacteria → antibody / spleen / complement; recurrent Neisseria → terminal complement; catalase-positive bacteria and fungi → phagocyte defect; and opportunistic infection (PCP, CMV, atypical mycobacteria) → T-cell defect / HIV. Remember the SPUR warning signs, test for HIV, and safety-net the at-risk patient (see vaccination).
🚨Test for HIV and never dismiss the asplenic or neutropenic patient. Opportunistic infections — PCP, oesophageal candidiasis, CMV, disseminated TB — are AIDS-defining and mandate an HIV test (see HIV). An asplenic / hyposplenic patient can develop overwhelming post-splenectomy pneumococcal sepsis (see sickle cell disease), and fever in neutropenia is neutropenic sepsis — a one-hour emergency (see neutropenic sepsis). Recurrent Neisseria infections point to terminal complement deficiency. Ensure vaccination and prophylaxis in the at-risk patient (see vaccination), and refer suspected primary immunodeficiency to immunology.

The infection history — site, organism, frequency, severity and response; the SPUR features (severe, persistent, unusual, recurrent); risk factors (HIV exposure, chemotherapy, splenectomy, steroids, diabetes); a family history of immunodeficiency or early infant deaths; and vaccination status
Examine
Growth / weight and nutrition; lymphoid tissue (nodes, tonsils, spleen); signs of chronic infection and bronchiectasis; skin (warts, abscesses, candida); and stigmata of underlying disease (myeloma, HIV)
Investigate
FBC + differential and blood film (neutropenia, Howell-Jolly bodies), HIV test, serum immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis, complement (CH50 / AP50), specific antibody / vaccine responses, and lymphocyte subsets; targeted microbiology and imaging
Act
Treat the acute infection (neutropenic / asplenic sepsis as emergencies); correct or manage the secondary cause; ensure vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis (asplenia, HIV); and refer suspected primary immunodeficiency to immunology for immunoglobulin replacement where indicated
Then — confirm the cause
HIV → HIV antigen / antibody testAntibody deficiency → serum immunoglobulinsNeutropenia → FBC differentialHyposplenism → film (Howell-Jolly bodies)Complement deficiency → CH50 / AP50Phagocyte defect (CGD) → neutrophil oxidative burst
The rules that carry it: think immunodeficiency when infections are severe, persistent, unusual or recurrent; let the organism name the defect; exclude the common secondary causes and test for HIV; and vaccinate, give prophylaxis and refer primary immunodeficiency to immunology.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis:
Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction with rapid-onset Airway, Breathing or Circulation compromise, usually with skin and mucosal changes — and the treatment is IM adrenaline, given first (see anaphylaxis).
  • Give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh (paediatric IM doses per Resus Council UK: 6–12 yr 300 micrograms, 6 months–6 yr 150 micrograms, under 6 months 100–150 micrograms), repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement, while managing ABC with high-flow oxygen, IV fluids and lying the patient flat with legs raised (see shock, breathlessness).
  • It is usually an IgE-mediated (type I) hypersensitivity reaction (see hypersensitivity reactions) to foods (nuts, shellfish), drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, contrast), venom or latex. Distinguish it from isolated urticaria / angioedema without ABC compromise (see urticaria).
  • Beware a biphasic reaction, take timed mast cell tryptase samples, and refer to allergy with an adrenaline auto-injector and plan.
🚨Anaphylaxis is a treat-first emergency — give IM adrenaline before anything else. Sudden Airway (swelling, stridor, hoarse voice), Breathing (wheeze, hypoxia) or Circulation (hypotension, collapse) problems after a trigger, usually with skin changes, are anaphylaxis — give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh and call for help (see anaphylaxis). Do not delay for antihistamines or steroids, and do not give adrenaline IV in this setting outside expert hands. Lie the patient flat with legs raised (or sit up if breathing is the problem), repeat adrenaline after 5 minutes, and give IV fluids. Observe for a biphasic reaction for 6–12 hours, and never send a patient home without two adrenaline auto-injectors and allergy referral.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Airway / breathing compromise
  • Stridor, hoarse voice, tongue / lip swelling (angioedema), wheeze, hypoxia
  • Give IM adrenaline now, high-flow oxygen, and call anaesthetics for the airway (see anaphylaxis)
  • Sit the patient up if breathing is the main problem (see breathlessness)
🚩Circulatory collapse (anaphylactic shock)
  • Hypotension, tachycardia and collapse after a trigger
  • IM adrenaline, IV fluid bolus, and lie flat with legs raised (see shock)
  • Repeat adrenaline every 5 minutes as needed; escalate to critical care
🟠Anaphylaxis — recognise & treat first
  • Sudden ABC compromise + usually skin / mucosal changes after a trigger
  • IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:1000), anterolateral thigh
  • Do not delay for antihistamines or steroids; oxygen and fluids alongside
🟠Triggers & mechanism
  • IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity (see hypersensitivity reactions)
  • Foods (nuts, shellfish), drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, contrast), venom, latex
  • Non-IgE and idiopathic anaphylaxis also occur — identify and avoid the trigger
🩹Biphasic & refractory anaphylaxis
  • A biphasic reaction can recur within 72 hours — observe 6–12 hours
  • Refractory anaphylaxis → an adrenaline infusion and critical care
  • Beta-blockers may blunt the response — consider glucagon
🩹Mimics & after-care
  • Isolated urticaria / angioedema without ABC compromise is not anaphylaxis (see urticaria)
  • A vasovagal faint (bradycardia, pallor, quick recovery) can mimic collapse
  • Timed mast cell tryptase, allergy referral, auto-injector and a written plan
Adrenaline first, and IM. The single intervention that saves life is prompt IM adrenaline — antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts that treat nothing acutely. Recognise the ABC picture after a trigger, treat immediately, and observe for a biphasic reaction.

ABC plus a trigger equals anaphylaxis. The reaction is sudden, systemic and usually accompanied by skin changes; isolated urticaria or angioedema without airway, breathing or circulatory compromise is not anaphylaxis and does not need adrenaline. When in doubt with ABC involvement, give it.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — recognise ABC compromise after a trigger, give IM adrenaline, then confirm and refer
History & red flags
The trigger and timing (food, drug, venom, latex, exercise); the speed of onset; airway, breathing and circulatory symptoms; skin / mucosal changes; previous reactions and known allergies; asthma and beta-blocker use; and any prior use of an auto-injector
Examine
A rapid ABCDE assessment — airway swelling / stridor, wheeze and oxygen saturations, blood pressure and perfusion, conscious level, and the skin (urticaria, angioedema, flushing); reassess continuously after treatment

A clinical diagnosis — do not delay treatment for tests; take timed mast cell tryptase (at presentation, at 1–2 hours, and at ≥24 hours); later, allergy testing (specific IgE, skin-prick) identifies the trigger
Act
IM adrenaline first, oxygen, IV fluids and positioning; repeat adrenaline at 5 minutes; adjunctive non-sedating antihistamine; treat refractory cases with an adrenaline infusion / critical care; observe for a biphasic reaction; and discharge with an auto-injector, training and allergy referral

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes / The Poi:
The poisoned patient is managed ABCDE first, then by recognising the toxidrome and consulting TOXBASE for specific antidotes and thresholds (see drug overdose & toxicology). The classic toxidromes are named by the vital signs, pupils and skin: opioid (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, reduced consciousness → naloxone), sympathomimetic (mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, sweating), anticholinergic (hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, urinary retention, delirium), cholinergic (SLUDGE, miosis, bradycardia → atropine) and sedative / hypnotic (reduced consciousness, respiratory depression). Some specific poisons are killers: paracetamol (timed level + nomogram → N-acetylcysteine) (see analgesia), salicylate (tinnitus, mixed acid-base) and tricyclic antidepressants (broad QRS, seizures, arrhythmia → sodium bicarbonate) (see seizures). Assess intent and treat self-harm risk (see depressive disorders); many events are accidental adverse drug reactions (see adverse drug reactions).
🚨Resuscitate ABCDE, check the glucose and an ECG, and phone TOXBASE. An opioid toxidrome (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, reduced consciousness) reverses with naloxone — support the airway (see reduced consciousness). Tricyclic overdose causes a broad QRS, arrhythmia and seizures — give sodium bicarbonate (see drug overdose & toxicology). Paracetamol is often asymptomatic early yet lethal late — always check a timed paracetamol level and treat on the nomogram (or empirically if staggered / unknown timing). Salicylate gives tinnitus and a mixed acid-base picture. Do not be reassured by an early normal examination — and always assess self-harm risk (see depressive disorders).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Airway / breathing failure (opioid & sedative)
  • Reduced consciousness + respiratory depression ± pinpoint pupils (opioid)
  • Support the airway and breathing; give naloxone for opioid toxicity (see reduced consciousness)
  • Sedative / hypnotic (benzodiazepine, alcohol, GHB) also depresses breathing
🚩Life-threatening specific poisons (TCA / salicylate)
  • Tricyclic — broad QRS, arrhythmia, seizures → sodium bicarbonate (see seizures)
  • Salicylate — tinnitus, hyperventilation, mixed acid-base → alkalinise urine / haemodialysis
  • Consult TOXBASE / the National Poisons Information Service (see drug overdose & toxicology)
🟠Recognise the toxidrome
  • Opioid (miosis) vs sympathomimetic / anticholinergic (mydriasis) — the pupils help
  • Anticholinergic is hot and dry; cholinergic is wet (SLUDGE) with bradycardia
  • The vital signs, pupils and skin name the class and its antidote
🟠Paracetamol overdose
  • Often asymptomatic early — hepatotoxicity is delayed
  • Check a timed paracetamol level and treat on the nomogram (see analgesia)
  • Staggered or unknown-timing overdose → treat empirically with N-acetylcysteine
🩹Cholinergic / organophosphate
  • SLUDGE / DUMBELS, miosis, bradycardia and bronchorrhoea
  • Give atropine (± pralidoxime); decontaminate and protect staff
  • Insecticides and nerve agents are the classic causes
🩹Approach, TOXBASE & intent
  • ABCDE, glucose, ECG, paracetamol & salicylate levels, venous gas
  • Consult TOXBASE for antidotes and thresholds (see drug overdose & toxicology)
  • Assess intent and self-harm risk; some are accidental ADRs (see depressive disorders, adverse drug reactions)

Pupils and skin split the toxidromes. Pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression mean opioid; big pupils with a dry skin mean anticholinergic and with a wet skin plus bradycardia mean cholinergic. Match the pattern to the antidote, and never skip the paracetamol level and ECG.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — resuscitate ABCDE, recognise the toxidrome, consult TOXBASE, and assess intent
History & red flags
What, how much, when and by what route; co-ingestants (alcohol, paracetamol); staggered vs single; the intent and a self-harm / mental-health history; regular medications and access to them; and a collateral history from ambulance, family and empty packets
Examine
ABCDE with GCS, pupils, skin (dry vs sweaty), temperature, heart rate and rhythm, blood pressure, respiratory rate and bladder; look for the pattern of a toxidrome and for signs of trauma or aspiration
Investigate
Capillary glucose and a 12-lead ECG (QRS / QT); timed paracetamol and salicylate levels, venous / arterial gas, U&E, LFTs, clotting, osmolar gap and a pregnancy test; specific drug levels (lithium, digoxin) as guided by TOXBASE
Act
Supportive care and airway protection; specific antidotes — naloxone (opioid), N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol), sodium bicarbonate (TCA / salicylate), atropine (cholinergic), flumazenil rarely; consider decontamination (activated charcoal <1 hour) and enhanced elimination; and a psychiatric / risk assessment before discharge (see depressive disorders)
Then — confirm the cause
Opioid toxidrome → clinical + response to naloxoneParacetamol overdose → timed level (nomogram)Salicylate poisoning → salicylate level + gasTricyclic toxicity → ECG (QRS width)Organophosphate → clinical + response to atropineAny overdose → TOXBASE + ABCDE
The rules that carry it: resuscitate ABCDE, check a glucose and ECG, recognise the toxidrome from the vitals, pupils and skin, send a timed paracetamol level, follow TOXBASE for antidotes, and assess self-harm risk before discharge.
